units.summary: Within the 2016 retirement cohort, individuals who did and did not contribute to mandatory or private pension schemes are compared on their retirement savings gap, with identification resting on a rich vector of demographic, income, wealth and pension-wealth controls rather than on any exogenous shift.
units.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation across the 2016 retirement cohort in whether and how much the individual contributed to mandatory (labour market) and private pension schemes. No reform, instrument or discontinuity is used; the paper reports the estimates as associations.

units.summary: Among retirees with essentially no mandatory pension contributions, observed differences in private pension contributions are related to the savings gap conditional on demographics, income and wealth, so identification comes purely from assumed conditional independence.
units.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation in private pension contributions within the subsample of 2016 retirees with almost no mandatory pension contributions.

units.summary: A collective agreement extended occupational pension schemes so that mandatory contribution rates rose steeply for some occupations and barely at all for others, and consumption and non-retirement wealth changes between the pre- and post-period are compared between the high- and low-increase occupation groups.
units.source_of_variation: The 1991 collective agreement extending occupational pension schemes to the private sector, which raised mandatory contribution rates sharply for some occupations (blue- and white-collar industry workers, from close to 0 percent in 1993 to 12 percent in 2009) and barely at all for others (economists, lawyers, nursery staff, teachers). Individuals are ranked by the average annual increase in their mandatory contribution rate 1996-2010.

units.summary: Person-year variation in the mandatory labour-market contribution rate is related to the probability of private pension participation conditional on income, wealth and demographics, with the quadratic relation reported as a conditional correlation rather than a causal effect.
units.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional and over-time variation in mandatory contribution rates across person-years 1999-2015; no reform, instrument or discontinuity.

units.summary: Hour-to-hour swings in Danish wind power output, driven by weather and conditional on calendar dummies and temperature, shift the hourly retail price and instrument households' price elasticity of electricity demand.
units.instrument: hourly wind power production W_t, measured in MWh
units.source_of_variation: Hourly variation in realized Danish wind power generation (MWh), largely driven by exogenous wind speed, conditional on year, month, day-of-week and hour-of-day dummies and the average daily temperature measured in Copenhagen.

units.summary: Regressing the hourly retail price on realized wind power production and temperature, conditional on year, month, day-of-week and hour dummies, documents how weather-driven supply shifts price under the assumption that wind output is unaffected by short-run demand.
units.source_of_variation: Hourly variation in realized Danish wind power generation (MWh), largely driven by exogenous wind speed, conditional on year, month, day-of-week and hour-of-day dummies and the average daily temperature measured in Copenhagen.

units.summary: Deaths of founding team members and of their children, fathers and mothers in the first three years after founding, together with the presence of co-residing family relations in the team, are used as instruments that shift new venture team stability without otherwise affecting ten-year firm size, identifying stability's effect in an instrumented Tobit.
units.instrument: Presence of family relations (number of founding NVT members living in the same household at startup); Own death in NVT; Child death in NVT; Father death in NVT; Mother death in NVT
units.source_of_variation: Variation in NVT stability driven by family constellations in the founding team and by deaths of NVT members, their children, fathers and mothers in the first 3 years after founding.

units.summary: Observed differences in team stability across ventures are related to ten-year firm size in a Tobit model with controls and year and municipality fixed effects, so identification rests on stability being unrelated to unobserved growth determinants given those covariates.
units.source_of_variation: Variation in NVT stability driven by family constellations in the founding team and by deaths of NVT members, their children, fathers and mothers in the first 3 years after founding.

units.summary: The average schooling of the founding team is varied across otherwise identical representative ventures within the estimated Tobit, so its association with predicted ten-year survival and conditional firm size is identified only by conditioning on the model's other covariates and fixed effects.
units.source_of_variation: Variation in the average years of education of the new venture team across ventures, holding the other characteristics of the representative venture fixed; education enters the instrumented Tobit as a control variable and is not itself instrumented.

units.summary: Within the same school, children tested on different dates inside the ministry's two- to three-month field window have accumulated different months of schooling at a given age, so school fixed effects plus birth-date variation separate exposure from age in explaining conscientiousness and reading scores and their SES gradients.
units.source_of_variation: Differential Exposure Approach: within-school variation in the date on which the mandatory survey/reading test is administered inside the Ministry of Education's two- to three-month field period, combined with a fixed school starting date (second week of August of the year the child turns six) and variation in birth dates, which separates months of school exposure from months of age.

units.summary: The same within-school comparison of children tested at different dates in the national field period identifies the effect of accumulated months of schooling on math test scores.
units.source_of_variation: Differential Exposure Approach applied to the national math test.

units.summary: Restricting to test dates between the winter holiday and Easter, within-school differences in testing date give exposure variation uncontaminated by school breaks, identifying schooling's effect on reading comprehension.
units.source_of_variation: Differential Exposure Approach on a sample restricted to test dates between the winter holiday and Easter, so that no school break falls inside the exposure window.

units.summary: With school start fixed to the year a child turns six, conditionally random birth dates make children in the same school differ in age at a given test date, identifying how age (as opposed to schooling) affects reading scores and whether its effect varies with parental education.
units.source_of_variation: Differential Exposure Approach: variation in birth dates given fixed school starting dates, interacted with parental education.

units.summary: Within each calibrated version of the directed-search model, the flat benefit is varied across steady states and the model-implied unemployment rates of each worker type and stable workers' welfare are read off the comparative statics.
units.source_of_variation: Comparative statics: the flat benefit g is varied across steady states in each of the four scenarios.

units.summary: Five free parameters of the two-type directed-search model are identified by exactly matching five observed moments—type-specific unemployment rates and imputed consumption gaps—so that worker-type differences in productivity and opportunity cost are recovered relative to normalised stable workers.
units.source_of_variation: Cross-type differences in unemployment rates and in imputed consumption moments, mapped into model parameters by matching five moments with five free parameters.

units.summary: Four calibrated economies differing only in the assumed source of marginal workers' higher unemployment are each simulated over a grid of benefit levels, and the welfare-maximising benefit is compared across these alternative parameterisations.
units.source_of_variation: Comparison across four calibrated model economies that differ in the assumed source of marginal workers' higher unemployment; within each, the flat benefit g is varied and total steady state welfare is maximised.

units.summary: Steady states of the calibrated model are simulated with the benefit at zero versus its welfare-maximising level, and across heterogeneity scenarios, to compute the model-implied changes in aggregate unemployment, output and productivity loss.
units.source_of_variation: Simulated steady states of the calibrated model under different benefit levels and heterogeneity scenarios.

units.summary: Inside the calibrated model exactly one marginal-worker parameter at a time is reset to its stable-worker value with all others held fixed, so the resulting drop in marginal workers' simulated unemployment rate attributes unemployment to that single channel.
units.source_of_variation: A counterfactual change of exactly one marginal-worker parameter to its stable-worker value inside the calibrated directed-search model, holding all other parameters constant.

units.summary: Worker and year fixed effects isolate within-worker, within-year variation in the share of the year spent unemployed, so the consumption drop associated with unemployment is estimated from the same worker's own movements in and out of unemployment rather than from cross-worker differences.
units.source_of_variation: Within-worker, within-year variation in the annual unemployment rate across the years 2008-2018.

units.summary: In a simplified model with stable workers' parameters normalised and separation rates equalised, exactly one marginal-worker parameter is varied in turn to reproduce the same observed unemployment gap, showing that the three scenarios are distinguished only by their implied consumption patterns across employment states.
units.source_of_variation: A simplified version of the model in which stable workers' parameters are normalised (z_s = 0, b_s = 0.9, h_s = 0), the vacancy cost c is calibrated to stable workers' 3% unemployment rate, separation-rate heterogeneity is removed (delta_s = delta_m) and exactly one marginal-worker parameter is varied to match their 35% unemployment rate.

units.summary: Dividing the observed status correlation for one kinship pair (e.g. in-laws or spouses) by that for another pair cancels the common classical-measurement-error attenuation, so the ratio of observed correlations identifies the correlation in underlying social status.
units.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation: the underlying correlation is identified by dividing the observed correlation between relatives at one place in the family tree by that between relatives at another, so that the common measurement-error attenuation θ cancels. Here unweighted average of the kinship-ratio estimates.

units.outcome: simulated true status of focal person
units.summary: A one-million-draw simulation imposes a known parent-child and marital correlation of 0.8 in underlying status, so the kinship-ratio estimator applied to the simulated observed statuses can be checked against the known truth.
units.source_of_variation: Simulation with a known data-generating process: underlying status is drawn with a parent-child and marital correlation of 0.8, so the ratio estimator can be compared with a known truth.

units.summary: Restricting to male relatives and using education or income as status indicators, the ratio of observed correlations between relatives at different family-tree positions cancels the shared measurement-error attenuation and identifies the underlying status correlation.
units.source_of_variation: Ratios of observed correlations between relatives at different positions in the family tree, restricted to male relatives, so that the common measurement-error attenuation cancels.

units.summary: Size profiles are attributed to firm age, calendar period and entry cohort by estimating the non-linear components of all three dimensions and allocating the two collinear linear trends under the preferred restriction of no linear time trend, so the 1950s cohorts' size advantage is read as a cohort rather than an age or period effect.
units.source_of_variation: A partial-identification approach to the age-period-cohort problem (Fosse and Winship, 2019): age, period and cohort dummies plus two estimated linear trends, with the linear trends allocated by the preferred restriction of no linear time trend (pi = 0).

units.summary: The age-size relation is identified from how the same firm's size changes as it ages, with a firm fixed effect absorbing time-invariant quality, sector and entry cohort and aggregate GDP growth plus an exit-year indicator standing in for time dummies to sidestep age-period-cohort collinearity.
units.source_of_variation: Within-firm variation in size as the same firm ages, net of the aggregate GDP growth rate and an exit-year indicator; no natural experiment is claimed.

units.summary: Because the 1964 universal daycare act led parishes to open their first daycare centre in different years, mothers' labour supply in early-opening neighbourhoods is compared with that in later-opening ones before and after each opening, under parallel trends.
units.source_of_variation: the staggered roll-out of daycare centres across Danish neighbourhoods (parishes) following the 1964 Act transforming targeted care into universal daycare, which took effect from 1966; time and regional variation in the year the first daycare opened in a parish

units.summary: Mothers' labour market outcomes are traced in event time around the year the first daycare centre opened in their parish, with the pre-opening path serving as the counterfactual for the post-opening dynamics.
units.source_of_variation: the staggered roll-out of daycare centres across Danish neighbourhoods (parishes) following the 1964 Act transforming targeted care into universal daycare, which took effect from 1966; time and regional variation in the year the first daycare opened in a parish

units.summary: Identification comes from year-to-year movements within a firm in the share of its job posts demanding digital (or data science/AI) skills, entered as a continuous dosage at leads and lags once firm and year-by-industry-by-region fixed effects and a pre-period IT-intensity trend are absorbed, so only within-firm deviations from common local-industry trends drive estimated employment responses.
units.source_of_variation: within-firm variation over 2008–2019 in the share of a firm's vacancies requiring digital skills, entered as a continuous treatment dosage at leads and lags k = -4,...,+4, conditional on firm fixed effects, year-by-industry-by-region fixed effects and a trend in the firm's 2008 share of employees with an IT degree

units.summary: Firms whose vacancy-based digital skill demand first exceeds a fixed share of their workforce in 2012–2014 are compared, in event time, with firms that cross the same threshold at least five years later, so the identifying assumption is that early and late adopters would have followed parallel employment paths absent the event.
units.source_of_variation: the first year in which a firm posts vacancies including any digital skill exceeding 7.5% of its full-time-equivalent employment (3.25% for data science & AI skills), for events in 2012–2014, with firms experiencing similar events five or more years later as controls

units.summary: Because the 14 major literary awards are announced at different dates, loans of a just-awarded title (and of the author's other titles) are compared week by week with loans of titles that were only nominated or that win an award later, so the staggered announcement timing supplies the counterfactual trend.
units.source_of_variation: Staggered timing of the announcement of major Danish literary awards (14 award events in the award-title analysis, July 2021 to December 2022), compared with nominated/short-listed titles and titles that win an award later (not-yet-treated)

units.outcome: weekly loans of author's other books
units.summary: The 210 newspaper reviews appear at different dates, so loans of the reviewed author's other books after a positive, mediocre or negative review are compared with loans of books by authors not yet reviewed in the same weeks.
units.source_of_variation: Staggered timing of the publication of literary reviews in national Danish newspapers (210 review events, July 2021 to December 2022), compared with not-yet-reviewed authors’ books over the same weeks

units.summary: Holding the worker-firm spell fixed and absorbing firm-year and female-year shocks, the paper compares how antidepressant use of women versus men in the same firm responds to within-spell changes in the firm's trade-weighted overlap of business hours with its foreign partners.
units.source_of_variation: Variation over time in the firm's trade-weighted business hours overlap with its foreign buyers and suppliers WITHIN a given worker-firm (job) spell, combined with the contrast between female and male workers employed by the same firm in the same year

units.summary: Within worker-firm spells and net of firm-year and female-year effects, the response of antidepressant use to changes in the firm's business hours overlap is compared across workers whose first occupation differs in O*NET-measured temporal flexibility.
units.source_of_variation: Variation over time in the firm's trade-weighted business hours overlap within a worker-firm spell, interacted with the (time-invariant) O*NET characteristics of the worker's first reported occupation: an alternative identification strategy based on occupational differences in temporal flexibility rather than on gender

units.summary: Trade Council caseworkers contact firms in alphabetical order, so a call from a country with lower business hours overlap than the firm's current export portfolio is a quasi-random shock to the firm's time-zone exposure, and its differential effect on women's versus men's antidepressant use within the same firm identifies the effect.
units.source_of_variation: Quasi-random calls from Danish Trade Council caseworkers based at embassies and consulates, who approach Danish firms sequentially in alphabetical order to sell export promotion services; the shock is a call from a country whose business hours overlap is below the firm's lagged export-weighted business hours overlap

units.summary: Denmark's 2002 extension of job-protected parental leave applied uniformly to all private employers, so comparing the pre-post change in employees' leave weeks at foundation-owned firms with that at observably matched family-owned firms isolates how ownership form shapes the take-up response to the same entitlement change.
units.source_of_variation: Denmark's 2002 parental leave reform, which extended job-protected, income-compensated leave from 26 to 52 weeks per birth and applied uniformly to all private-sector employers, interacted with firm ownership form (foundation-owned vs family-owned firms (owner-managed or with a family majority on the board)); coarsened exact matching (CEM) on pre-reform ln(assets), ln(employment), ln(firm age), industry, leverage and export share, retaining 40 percent of the sample

units.summary: Adult children who suddenly and unexpectedly lose a first parent are compared in event time with nearest-neighbour matched individuals whose parents survive the window, so the death's timing identifies its effect on employment and earnings under parallel trends and no anticipation.
units.source_of_variation: the timing of sudden, unexpected first parental deaths in 1985-2014, compared with nearest-neighbor matched controls who do not lose a parent within the five-year window

units.summary: Event-time coefficients around the sudden parental death are estimated without a control group, relying on variation in age at the death together with age-by-year and education-by-year controls to trace employment, earnings and mental-health prescriptions.
units.source_of_variation: variation in age at the time of the first parental death, with age-by-year and education-by-year controls; no control group

units.summary: Incumbent workers' wage growth is compared before and after their employer reports offshoring or backshoring in successive firm surveys, against incumbents in never-internationalizing firms, with worker, industry and time fixed effects and separate urban/rural estimates.
units.source_of_variation: Within-worker changes over time in the employing firm's reported offshoring and backshoring status, from three Statistics Denmark VOUT firm surveys (2007, 2011, 2016, covering 2001–2006, 2009–2011 and 2014–2016), compared with incumbent workers in non-internationalizing firms, separately for urban and rural firm locations

units.summary: Identification rests only on mutually adjusted Poisson regression: cross-sectional and between-season differences in demographic, socioeconomic and clinical characteristics among individuals with type 1 diabetes are related to vaccination uptake and persistence, assuming the entered covariates capture confounding.
units.source_of_variation: Observed cross-sectional and between-season variation in demographic, socioeconomic and clinical characteristics among individuals with T1D; there is no reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument -- the paper reports mutually adjusted associations, not an exogenous shock

units.summary: Children registered with social services for maltreatment are compared on health-service use and adult benefit and employment outcomes with a propensity-score-matched cohort of children not known to social services, so identification rests entirely on matching and conditional ignorability rather than on any exogenous shift in maltreatment.
units.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used: children known to social services (recorded on the child protection register or as children looked after) are compared with a propensity-matched cohort of children not known to social services

units.summary: Each retiree's observed net home equity is mechanically converted into a life annuity using an imposed interest rate and an aggregate life-expectancy figure, and the resulting payout is added to observed retirement income to simulate counterfactual net replacement rates across income and wealth deciles, with alternative interest-rate and lower-equity scenarios as sensitivity variants.
units.source_of_variation: none observed: the counterfactual is generated by deterministically annuitising each individual's observed net home equity at retirement under equation (1) and adding the payout to observed retirement income

units.summary: Half of surveyed job seekers were randomly shown the actual average re-employment wage of their demographic cell, so comparing treated and untreated respondents (within prior-belief groups) identifies the causal effect of the information on stated wage expectations, reservation wages and search behaviour.
units.source_of_variation: Random assignment of a random half of main-survey respondents to receive information on the actual average monthly re-employment wage of job seekers in their own demographic cell (survey information-provision experiment fielded from 23 October 2023)

atlas.from_label: Information about re-employment wages of comparable workers

units.summary: The randomized information treatment indicators, interacted with prior-perception-gap groups, serve as instruments for the respondent's expected wage, so only the belief shift induced by the experiment identifies the effect of wage expectations on reservation wages and search behaviour.
units.instrument: Randomized information treatment indicators (interacted with the prior-perception-gap groups)
units.source_of_variation: Random assignment of a random half of main-survey respondents to receive information on the actual average monthly re-employment wage of job seekers in their own demographic cell (survey information-provision experiment fielded from 23 October 2023)

units.summary: The model's latent transmission parameters are identified from the covariances of education and long-run outcome ranks across father, mother and two siblings within each family quartet, with the sibling-shared component pinned down by same- versus mixed-gender sibling pairs under orthogonality restrictions on the latent factors.
units.source_of_variation: Covariance structure of education and long-run outcome percentile ranks across the four members of each family quartet (father, mother and the two first-born children); the sibling-shared component is identified from variation in sibling gender composition (same-gender versus mixed-gender pairs). No exogenous policy variation is used in the baseline model.

units.summary: The same within-family covariance model is estimated separately for families whose parents grew up near versus far from a middle school offering eighth and ninth grades, so differences in the estimated education and transmission parameters are attributed descriptively to parental schooling access rather than to a causal reform effect.
units.source_of_variation: The baseline model is estimated separately on families partitioned by parental access to middle schools, measured as the average of the mother's and father's distance at age 14 to the nearest middle school offering eighth and ninth grades, which varied across municipalities and cohorts with the gradual implementation of the 1937 school reform; the paper interprets the comparison descriptively rather than as the causal effect of the reform.

units.summary: Identification comes from year-to-year deviations of a practice's own lagged motivation score from its practice-specific mean in a Mundlak within-between random-effects model, so time-constant practice heterogeneity is absorbed and only within-practice changes in motivation are related to prescribing quality, conditional on patient, practice and area characteristics and time dummies.
units.source_of_variation: Year-to-year changes in a practice's own average lagged motivation score around its practice-specific mean (the practice-demeaned term M_it-1 - M-bar_i) in a within-between (Mundlak/hybrid) random-effects panel model. There is no exogenous shock or reform; the authors explicitly decline a causal reading.

units.summary: Identification rests on comparing prescribing quality across general practices that differ in their practice-average lagged motivation, conditional on observed patient, practice and area characteristics and time dummies, with no exogenous shock and unobserved confounding acknowledged.
units.source_of_variation: Differences in practice-average lagged motivation across general practices (the term M-bar_i) in a within-between (Mundlak/hybrid) random-effects panel model, conditional on observed patient, practice and area characteristics. There is no exogenous shock or reform; the authors explicitly decline a causal reading.

units.summary: Realized asset and gross-profit growth are compared between firms with older and younger CEOs, conditioning on observed CEO and firm characteristics within industry, with no exogenous variation in CEO age.
units.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation in CEO age across the surveyed firms, within industry.

units.summary: Because the vignette's project attributes are orthogonally randomized, their effect on the attractiveness rating can be estimated separately for CEOs aged 60+ and younger CEOs, identifying how an observed age group moderates the experimental effect.
units.source_of_variation: Orthogonal randomization of the vignette attributes, interacted with the observed (not randomized) CEO 60 or older indicator.

units.summary: Within the risk-module subsample, elicited and perceived risk attitudes and vignette ratings are compared between CEOs aged 60+ and younger CEOs conditional on observed controls.
units.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation in CEO age within the 2133-respondent risk-module subsample, with the project attributes randomized.

units.summary: The portion of a CEO's vignette rating not explained by the randomized project attributes is used as an inaction-propensity measure and related to the firm's realized growth conditional on observed controls.
units.source_of_variation: Cross-CEO variation in the residual from the experimental first-stage regression, i.e. the part of a CEO's vignette rating not explained by the randomized project attributes.

units.summary: Each CEO rates an independently randomized hypothetical project, so the age gap in attractiveness ratings cannot be driven by differences in project characteristics, although CEO age itself is only adjusted for by observed controls.
units.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation in CEO age across 3751 surveyed CEOs, combined with orthogonal randomization of the project attributes within the vignette so that project characteristics are held constant by design rather than only by control.

units.summary: Orthogonal random draws of the vignette's worst/base/best-case returns, probabilities and payout period vary the implied mean, dispersion and skewness of returns across CEOs, identifying their causal effect on the rated attractiveness of the project.
units.source_of_variation: Orthogonal randomization of the vignette's worst/base/best-case returns, probabilities and payout period, from which the first three moments of the implied IRR distribution and the time horizon are computed; parameters were drawn from discrete distributions scaled by a firm-size factor.

units.summary: The age gap in vignette ratings is estimated with the randomized project attributes and their interactions with the age indicator included, so project characteristics are neutralized by design while age is handled by conditioning on observables.
units.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation in CEO age combined with orthogonal randomization of project attributes; column 3 adds interactions of the age indicator with each standardized attribute.

units.summary: Because register data cover the full sampling universe, the CEO-age gradient in realized firm investment is estimated separately for survey respondents and non-respondents to check whether selection into the survey biases the main estimates.
units.source_of_variation: Variation in whether a firm's CEO returned the survey, within the sampling universe.

units.summary: Older workers who separate from establishments cutting employment by more than 30% in a base year are compared, around the displacement date, with propensity-score-matched never-displaced households, so the firm-level shock rather than worker characteristics drives the timing of job loss.
units.source_of_variation: Involuntary job separation in a mass layoff: employment at the establishment of the worker's main employment drops by more than 30% in the displacement base year t* (2013-2017) and the worker separates from that employer; private establishments with at least 20 employees; treated households matched 1:1 by propensity score to never-treated households

units.summary: Children whose father's criminal act, charge or conviction fell within a year before the national test are compared, conditional on child and parental characteristics, with children whose father experienced the same justice-system event within a year after the test, so the only difference is whether the event preceded the test date.
units.source_of_variation: Variation in the timing of the standardized test date relative to the timing of the father's first incarceration, within cohort groups.

units.summary: Children who experienced their father's first incarceration within a year before the national test are compared with children whose father is incarcerated within a year after the test, with the near-random spacing of the test date relative to the incarceration providing the variation in exposure.
units.source_of_variation: Variation in the timing of the standardized test date relative to the timing of the father's first incarceration: children who experienced PI within 1 year before the test are compared with children who experience it within 1 year after the test.

units.summary: Self-selected sports participants are compared with inactive pupils on later school-related social well-being using augmented inverse probability weighting on thirteen covariates measured in the prior wave, so identification rests entirely on conditional ignorability (which the authors say does not hold).
units.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is exploited: voluntary, self-selected participation in organized leisure-time sports is compared across pupils after adjusting for observed covariates measured at T − 1 by augmented inverse probability weighting. The authors state explicitly that this does not identify a causal effect.

units.summary: Siblings graduating from the same families are compared, so that sibling fixed effects absorb shared, time-constant family factors and only the within-family difference in teachers' subjective scores drives the comparison of post-compulsory educational choices.
units.source_of_variation: Differences in teacher scores between siblings who graduated from grade 9 in the 2005-2009 cohorts, holding constant everything common between siblings and constant over time via sibling fixed effects

units.summary: Because each pupil is graded twice in the same subject, once subjectively by teachers and once by external examiners, the group difference in grades is differenced across the two assessment schemes, so that the remaining gap reflects grading disparities rather than ability differences.
units.source_of_variation: The data structure with two scores for each pupil and subject area - a subjective teacher score and an externally examined exam score - differenced across type of assessment on the one hand and across gender, parental education and ethnicity on the other

atlas.to_label: teacher scores relative to exam scores

units.summary: The estimated grading gaps are combined with the estimated effect of teacher scores on schooling choices to compute, by accounting, how disadvantaged pupils' choice probabilities would change if teachers graded them like the advantaged comparison group.
units.source_of_variation: A two-step simulation: the estimated grading gaps (difference-in-differences, Table 2) give the counterfactual teacher scores, and the sibling fixed effects estimates (Table 4) translate them into predicted changes in choice probabilities

units.summary: The gap between a pupil's subjective teacher score and the external exam score is compared across pupil groups while controlling continuously for the exam score, so identification rests on the exam score fully capturing ability rather than on differencing across assessment schemes.
units.source_of_variation: The data structure with two scores for each pupil and subject area - a subjective teacher score and an externally examined exam score - differenced across type of assessment on the one hand and across gender, parental education and ethnicity on the other; in this robustness specification ability is controlled for continuously instead of by quintile split, which footnote 31 notes is no longer a difference-in-difference specification

atlas.to_label: teacher scores relative to exam scores

units.summary: In the survey subsample, teacher scores are related to schooling choices while directly conditioning on the exam score and on survey-measured parental attitudes and educational preferences, which are assumed to stand in for the family factors absorbed by sibling fixed effects.
units.source_of_variation: Variation in teacher scores across pupils in the survey sample, conditional on survey-measured parental attitudes and preferences regarding the child's education and on the exam score

units.summary: Students who differ in years of tertiary education (a proxy for experience with and knowledge of the benefit rules) are compared within narrow DKK 4,000 earned-income bins and other covariates, so remaining differences in ending up in the dominated region reflect benefit take-up behaviour rather than earnings.
units.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional differences in experience with and knowledge of the student benefit system among students at risk of the dominated region in 2008, with earned income held fixed non-parametrically in bins of DKK 4,000 so that the remaining variation comes from benefit take-up behaviour

units.summary: The 2009 reform raised the student benefit income limit by DKK 21,900 and the phase-out rate from 52 to 62%, so the shift in the earnings distribution around the relocated kink between pre- and post-reform cross-sections — with lower income ranges as a placebo — identifies the labor supply elasticity.
units.source_of_variation: The 2009 reform of the Danish student benefit system, which increased the baseline income limit by DKK 21,900 and the phase-out rate from 52 to 62%

units.summary: At the baseline income limit the phase-out of student benefits makes the effective marginal tax rate jump from 42 to 72%, so a frictionless model with a positive elasticity predicts sharp excess mass in the earnings distribution there; the observed absence of bunching at this kink identifies optimization frictions.
units.source_of_variation: The kink in the budget set at the baseline income limit, where the effective marginal tax rate jumps from 42 to 72%
